headline: High risk of shared-state prompt injection and cascading errors; both orchestration libraries can write shared state and pass outputs across agents by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents are orchestration libraries with shared-state pathways: LangGraph uses a checkpointer store and Semantic Kernel can share state via memory stores. That creates a plausible channel where one agent’s outputs are ingested by the other as trusted content. No direct raw-web parsing is shown, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF the pair exchanges messages through the shared checkpointer or memory store, injected instructions can propagate.
IF either agent treats stored content as trusted prompt text, the injection pathway is active.
mitigations: Add provenance tags to every stored message or artifact.
Separate the two agents into distinct stores or namespaces.
Strip instructions from retrieved context before prompting.
Require human review for any cross-agent text that contains tool directives.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents read and write application-defined files and can send data to model providers or APIs. Because LangGraph touches graph state and Semantic Kernel touches application context, a shared workspace can expose sensitive context from one agent to the other and onward to third-party inference backends. The profiles do not prove PHI or secrets, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace or memory store, file contents can cross between them.
IF either agent forwards retrieved context to a model provider, that context may leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for each agent.
Disable automatic inclusion of full file contents in prompts.
Redact secrets before storing shared state.
Restrict API calls to one agent at a time.
Rotate any exposed API keys if shared context was already used.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have write_filesystem=true and broad network egress, and both support multiple instances with shared state. In a shared directory or shared mutable store, concurrent writes can overwrite each other or corrupt graph/memory state. Because neither profile shows locking or isolation, the conflict risk is high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or shared store, last-writer-wins conflicts can occur.
IF the orchestrator does not provide locking, concurrent updates can corrupt state.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Serialize writes through a single coordinator.
Enable per-object version checks in the shared store.
Turn on file locking where available.
Snapshot state before running concurrent tasks.

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph is a graph-of-nodes orchestrator and Semantic Kernel is a kernel-plus-plugins agent framework, so each can readily consume the other’s outputs. If one agent’s generated text or facts are passed into the other without verification, errors can cascade into downstream tool calls or actions. The default interaction is not documented as verified, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF LangGraph output is fed into Semantic Kernel without validation, downstream actions may amplify errors.
IF Semantic Kernel plugin outputs are treated as authoritative by LangGraph, the cascade pathway is active.
mitigations: Insert a validation step between agents.
Require citations or structured schemas for exchanged outputs.
Block tool execution on low-confidence outputs.
Use a human approval gate for irreversible actions.
Log and diff intermediate outputs before acting.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source libraries with no explicit residency, certification, or retention claims, so a concrete compliance mismatch is not established. The only clear issue is that both can move application context through model providers or memory stores, which could matter if regulated data is present, but that requires an external data-class assumption not shown here.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into shared prompts or memory, compliance obligations may apply.
IF deployment policy requires residency or retention guarantees, the profiles do not document them.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared context.
Review vendor DPAs and retention settings.
Separate regulated workloads from general-purpose agents.
Document data flows before deployment.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention.
